title: A week of Kalimpong homestays on ₹2,000 a day
meta_description: Seven nights in Kalimpong's homestay villages, Sillery Gaon, Pedong, Lava and Rishyap, on about ₹2,000 a day each, with a day-by-day cost table.
summary: Seven nights in the villages around Kalimpong cost about ₹14,000–14,500 per person if two travel together, close to ₹2,000 a day. The trick is homestays with dinner and breakfast included, shared jeeps between towns, shared cars only for the last climb, and walking between villages where a path exists.
key_takeaways: Homestays around Kalimpong charge about ₹1,300–2,200 per person with dinner and breakfast, which covers most of a day's spending.
Shared jeeps from Kalimpong's Motor Stand reach Pedong for ₹80–120 and Lava for ₹120–180, so a car is needed only for the last short climbs.
Two forest walks, Sillery Gaon down to Pedong and Lava up to Rishyap, replace car transfers and are the best hours of the week.
The plan assumes two people sharing cars and guides; a solo traveller should budget nearer ₹2,300–2,500 a day.

sections.heading: Why a week, and why villages
paras: Most visitors give Kalimpong a night or two in town and a quick drive to Deolo. The district rewards slower travel. Within an hour or two of the Motor Stand, farming families in a string of villages have opened spare rooms to guests, and they feed you what the house eats: rice, dal, a vegetable from the slope, squash or fern in season, pickle, and tea that keeps coming. The view from the courtyard is often one a town hotel could not offer at any price.

Villages also make a tight budget work. A homestay rate includes dinner and breakfast, so the biggest costs of the day are fixed before you arrive. There is little to spend money on once you are there except a guide for a walk and lunch. Transport is the variable, and that is where planning pays: link the villages so that shared jeeps do most of the work and your own feet do the rest.

A homestay day has its own rhythm. Tea arrives early, often before 6 am in the clear months, because the mountain view is best at dawn. Breakfast is puri and potato curry, bread and eggs, or noodles. The day is yours for walking; most hosts will pack a simple lunch or point you to a village shop. Dinner is served early, around 7 to 8 pm, often in the family kitchen beside the stove, and the village goes quiet soon after. Rooms are clean and simple, with heavy quilts; hot water may come in a bucket, and power cuts happen. Bring a torch, a warm layer, slippers for indoors and patience with patchy mobile signal.

sections.heading: The route in one line
paras: Siliguri to Kalimpong town for one night, then two nights in Sillery Gaon above Pedong, a walk down to Pedong for one night, back through Kalimpong by jeep to Lava for one night, a forest walk up to Rishyap for one night, a last night in Lava, and down to Siliguri on the eighth morning. That is seven nights, four beds and very little time in vehicles: no single day has more than about three and a half hours on the road.

The order matters. Sillery Gaon and Pedong sit east of town on one road, and Lava and Rishyap on another, so doing them as two loops from Kalimpong uses the cheap shared jeeps on the main roads and avoids paying for a car across country. If you have less time, cut the Lava half and you have a three- or four-night trip that keeps the same daily cost.

sections.heading: Day by day, with what it costs
paras: Figures are per person, assuming two people share rooms, cars and guides, and are indicative for 2025–26. Homestay rates include dinner and breakfast. Prices rise in October and on long weekends, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: The Pedong side: Sillery Gaon and Pedong
paras: From Kalimpong's Motor Stand, a morning jeep to Pedong takes about an hour for ₹80–120. From Pedong bazaar you need a local car for the 5–6 km climb to Sillery Gaon, about ₹500–800, which is why we split it. Sillery Gaon, at about 1,830 m, is the best known of the villages on this side, with Kanchenjunga at dawn on clear days. Its homestays charge about ₹1,400–2,200 per person with meals; book ahead for October and long weekends.

Spend the full second day on foot. Ramitey Dara, about 3 km away, is the viewpoint over the Teesta, where the river is seen bending again and again through the valley; locals usually say 14 bends, some count 11. A village guide costs ₹500–800 and is worth it for the forest path. On day four, send nothing ahead and simply walk down the road to Pedong with your daypack, about 5–6 km and mostly downhill. Pedong, at 1,240 m, is a small market town on the old trade route toward Tibet, with the ruins of Damsang fort, an old monastery and Cross Hill close by. Its homestays and lodges are a little cheaper, about ₹1,200–1,800 with meals.

sections.heading: The Lava side: Lava and Rishyap
paras: Day five is the only long transport day. Take a morning jeep from Pedong back to Kalimpong, then a jeep from the Motor Stand to Lava, ₹120–180 a seat and about 1.5 hours via Algarah. Lava jeeps are few and mostly leave in the morning, so do not dawdle. Lava, at about 2,200 m, is colder and greener than the Pedong side, a small bazaar and monastery town on the edge of Neora Valley National Park. Homestays here cost about ₹1,300–2,000 per person with meals; the WBFDC Lava Eco Tourism Centre is a fixed-tariff alternative at roughly ₹2,000–3,000 a room.

On day six, walk up to Rishyap by the forest path, about 4 km and steadily uphill through oak and rhododendron, with a guide for ₹600–1,000. Rishyap, at 2,591 m, is the highest village on this trip. Its Sherpa and Lepcha families began taking guests in 1998, and Tiffin Dara, about 1 km from the houses, shows the Kanchenjunga range end to end at sunrise. Next morning a shared car back down to Lava costs ₹800–1,200, split two ways, and you have the afternoon for the monastery or the weekly haat if it falls that day.

sections.heading: Where the money goes, and where it leaks
paras: About three quarters of the week's spending is beds and meals, and those are fixed. The leaks are elsewhere. Reserved cars are the biggest: a single unplanned car from Kalimpong to Lava costs ₹2,500–3,000, more than a whole day's budget for one person. Missing the morning jeep is how it usually happens, so plan to be at the Motor Stand by 8 am.

Packaged sightseeing is the second leak. Drivers in town offer point-to-point tours that string together viewpoints and nurseries; they are pleasant but not cheap. Bottled water adds up too, and every homestay will boil water for you if asked.
list: Book homestays by phone direct; the whole payment stays with the family.
Ask whether the rate includes lunch, and whether tea is extra.
Carry cash in small notes; few villages take cards and UPI can fail without network.
Travel solo and costs rise to about ₹2,300–2,500 a day, mostly from cars and guides.

sections.heading: When to go, and what can go wrong
paras: October to December and March to May are the best months, with clear mornings and dry paths. October is the busiest and dearest; November and early December are quieter and still clear, though nights at Lava and Rishyap drop near freezing, so bring a warm layer. In the monsoon, from June to September, paths turn slippery, leeches come out and landslides block roads, sometimes for days.

NH10 along the Teesta, the main road between Siliguri and Kalimpong, has had long closures and damage since the October 2023 flood, and jeeps have sometimes used longer roads. Build a spare half-day into the plan, ask your homestay about the roads the evening before each move, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can you really travel around Kalimpong on ₹2,000 a day?
faqs.a: Yes, if two people share cars and guides, stay in homestays with dinner and breakfast included, and use shared jeeps between towns. Our seven-night plan comes to about ₹14,150 per person, just over ₹2,000 a day. Solo travellers pay more for cars and guides, about ₹2,300–2,500 a day. October and long weekends push homestay rates up.

faqs.q: How much does a homestay cost in the Kalimpong villages?
faqs.a: Usually about ₹1,300–2,200 per person a night with dinner and breakfast, for 2025–26. Pedong and Lava sit at the lower end; well-placed houses in Sillery Gaon and Rishyap at the upper end, especially in October. Lunch is often extra at ₹150–250. Booking direct by phone is often a little cheaper than a listing site.

faqs.q: Are there shared jeeps to Sillery Gaon and Rishyap?
faqs.a: Not usefully. Shared jeeps run from Kalimpong's Motor Stand to Pedong for ₹80–120 and to Lava for ₹120–180, mostly in the morning. From Pedong to Sillery Gaon you need a local car, about ₹500–800, and Rishyap is reached by a car from Lava or by the 4 km forest path uphill. Your homestay host can arrange the car.

faqs.q: Is the Lava to Rishyap walk difficult?
faqs.a: It is a steady uphill walk of about 4 km through forest, from about 2,200 m to 2,591 m, and takes most people two to three hours with stops. Paths can be muddy, so wear shoes with grip. Take a local guide, ₹600–1,000, as junctions are not marked. Avoid it in heavy monsoon rain, when leeches and slippery stretches make it hard going.

faqs.q: What is the best time for a Kalimpong homestay trip?
faqs.a: October to December and March to May, when mornings are clear and paths dry. November and early December are quieter than October and still bright, though nights in Lava and Rishyap drop near freezing. The monsoon, June to September, brings landslides and road closures. NH10 has had long closures since October 2023, so check current status before you travel.
